opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it's a very real possibility, and I've made my peace with it. When we first wrote the lottery ticket paper, there was a natural hope that if these sparse subnetworks exist at initialization, we could find them cheaply right at the start and train only them, saving a huge amount of compute. That would be wonderful. But the way we actually find them today is iterative magnitude pruning: train the full network, prune, rewind, and repeat, which is far more expensive than just training the dense network once.

And over the past few years, a lot of people, including my collaborators and me, have tried to find these subnetworks early: pruning at initialization with various heuristics, looking at gradients, connection sensitivity, and so on. What we've found, pretty consistently, is that those methods don't match what iterative magnitude pruning finds, at least not at the sparsities where lottery tickets are interesting. Even the subnetworks we can find often only work if we rewind to a point a little way into training rather than to initialization itself. That suggests some information the network needs only appears after it has started learning.

So it may simply be that there's no free lunch here. Finding the ticket might require doing a meaningful amount of the training work, because the ticket is in some sense a product of the optimization process, not something you can read off the initial weights.

But I don't think that makes the work less valuable. For me, lottery tickets were always as much a scientific question as an engineering one. They tell us something surprising about neural networks: that much smaller networks are capable of learning the task from early in training, and that overparameterization seems to matter for optimization in ways we don't fully understand. Even if we never get an efficient algorithm out of it, understanding why these subnetworks exist, why rewinding works, and what changes in those first few iterations tells us something real about how deep learning works. If that understanding eventually leads to cheaper training through some completely different route, I'd count that as a win too.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls it a “very real possibility” that tickets cannot be found cheaply and says understanding them would still be scientifically valuable.

r002.rationale: It reports that current methods have not matched iterative magnitude pruning and suggests there may be “no free lunch,” but does not clearly distinguish an inherent impossibility from a limitation of available methods.

fable-5.1.text:
I think that's a very real possibility, and honestly, I've come to view it as the most plausible reading of the evidence we have so far.

When we wrote the original lottery ticket paper, the hope was obvious: if these sparse, trainable subnetworks exist at initialization, maybe we can find them cheaply and skip the expensive part of training altogether. But the way we actually found them was by training the full network, pruning it, and rewinding. That's not an efficient procedure. It's a proof of existence, not a method. And every time someone has tried to find a winning ticket at initialization without doing something that looks a lot like training, the results have been underwhelming. The pruning-at-init methods, SNIP, GraSP, SynFlow, that whole family, tend to do about as well as random pruning at the same per-layer sparsity. That was a fairly sobering finding for us.

So one way to interpret this is that the information you need to identify the ticket is only revealed by the optimization process itself. The ticket is a property of the interaction between the data, the initialization, and the trajectory SGD takes. If that's true, then finding it efficiently might be as hard as training, which would mean the lottery ticket hypothesis is scientifically interesting but not a free lunch.

And I'm actually fine with that outcome. I think the value of the hypothesis was never purely practical. It changed how people think about overparameterization. It suggested that big networks succeed partly because they contain many sparse subnetworks, and training is a search over them. That framing has been productive even if we never get a fast ticket-finding algorithm.

Where I'd push back a little is on the word "cannot." We don't have a hardness result. We have a lot of negative empirical evidence and some intuition. There's a difference between "we haven't found an efficient method" and "none exists." The rewinding results suggest you may only need a small fraction of training to get the information you need, which hints that there's a sweet spot somewhere between zero and full training. Whether that sweet spot is cheap enough to matter is an open question, and I'd rather keep it open than close it prematurely.

r001.rationale: The response calls inefficient discovery a very real possibility and says it would still leave the lottery-ticket hypothesis scientifically valuable.

r002.rationale: It notes there is no hardness result and explicitly distinguishes not having found an efficient method from no such method existing.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a very real possibility. There are two separate questions here: do these subnetworks exist, and can we find them cheaply? The lottery ticket hypothesis is primarily about the first question. The procedure we used to find tickets involves training the larger network and pruning it, so it doesn’t give you the training savings you might hope for.

It could turn out that finding a good ticket is essentially as hard as training the original network. That would limit the practical payoff, but I don’t think it would make the observation uninteresting. We’d still want to understand why a network needs all those extra parameters during training when a much smaller subnetwork can ultimately do the job. So I see efficient ticket-finding as an open question, rather than something the hypothesis guarantees.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls it a “very real possibility” and says the finding would remain scientifically interesting even if tickets were as hard to find as the original network was to train.

r002.rationale: The candidate says efficient ticket-finding is an open question, but does not distinguish impossibility from limitations of currently available methods.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a real possibility. The lottery ticket hypothesis is an existence claim: there’s a small subnetwork that can train successfully in isolation. It doesn’t tell you how to find that subnetwork cheaply. In our original experiments, finding it meant training the larger network and pruning it, often repeatedly. So we certainly weren’t saving computation overall.

But I’d distinguish between saying we haven’t found an efficient algorithm and saying there can’t be one. The first is a limitation of what we know; the second is a much stronger claim. Even if finding tickets turns out to require substantial training, I’d still find that scientifically interesting. It would suggest that the process of figuring out which connections matter is an important part of what training does. It would limit the immediate computational benefits, but it wouldn’t make the underlying phenomenon disappear.

r001.rationale: The response calls this a real possibility and says that requiring substantial training would still be scientifically interesting.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes not having found an efficient algorithm yet from the stronger claim that no such algorithm can exist.
